title: Governor of Arizona

context.text: Incumbent Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs is seeking a second term. She was unopposed in the Democratic primary.
Rep. Andy Biggs won the July 21 Republican primary with about 74% of the vote, ahead of Rep. David Schweikert (about 14%), Scott Neely (about 7%) and Ken Miceli (about 5%).
This is the first Arizona governor's election in which candidates run with a running mate for the new office of lieutenant governor, created by Proposition 131 in 2022.

The No Labels Party and Green Party also have nominees on the ballot. No Libertarian candidate qualified. The printed Maricopa County sample ballot lists exactly four governor-and-lieutenant-governor tickets.

candidates.name: Katie Hobbs
candidates.ballotNote: Running with John Giles, former mayor of Mesa. Unopposed in the Democratic primary.

summary.text: Katie Hobbs is the Democratic incumbent Governor of Arizona, seeking a second term with running mate John Giles, the former mayor of Mesa. A social worker by training, she served in the Arizona House and Senate and as Secretary of State before being elected governor in 2022.

background.text: Born in Phoenix and raised in Tempe; earned a bachelor's degree in social work from Northern Arizona University (1992) and a master's in social work from Arizona State University (1995).
Worked as a social worker and as chief compliance officer at the Sojourner Center, a domestic violence shelter; executive director of Emerge Arizona from 2013 to 2019.
Served one term in the Arizona House (elected 2010) and three terms in the Arizona Senate (elected 2012, 2014, 2016), including as Senate Minority Leader beginning in 2015.
Served as Arizona Secretary of State from January 2019 until she became governor in January 2023.

priorities.text: Protecting abortion and reproductive health care access, including repealing the pre-statehood abortion law.
priorities.quote: The decision to have a child should rest solely between a woman and her doctor, not the government or politicians.

priorities.text: Housing affordability: working with local governments to expand low-interest financing and incentives for affordable and workforce housing.
Border communities and public safety: more state funding and Department of Public Safety help for local law enforcement and border-area hospitals, alongside a call for federal immigration reform.
Education: free early childhood education and affordable child care, school counselors, and support for educators.

positions.summary: Her official priorities page lists repealing Arizona's 1901 abortion law and expanding access to family planning and abortion services, and says she will use her veto against restrictions.
Lists free early childhood education and affordable child care for parents among her education priorities.

Launched Operation SECURE, deploying the National Guard and state troopers to the border, while her official priorities call for federal immigration reform that includes a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants and DREAMers.

record.text: Signed the repeal of Arizona's 1864 near-total abortion ban, one day after the state Senate gave it final approval.

Issued Executive Order 2025-09 directing the state occupational safety division (ADOSH) to form a Workplace Heat Safety Task Force to draft heat-risk guidelines for employers, with final recommendations to go to the Industrial Commission of Arizona for approval.
Issued Executive Order 2025-12 directing state health officials to coordinate broad access to FDA-approved COVID-19 vaccines, including possible pharmacist standing orders.

Issued Executive Order 2025-15 directing the Department of Revenue to update state tax forms for a higher standard deduction and to publish instructions for tips, overtime, senior and car-loan-interest deductions if the Legislature adopts them.

candidates.name: Andy Biggs
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Sine Kerr, former state senator. Won the Republican primary with about 74% of the vote.

summary.text: Andy Biggs is the U.S. Representative for Arizona's 5th District, seeking the governorship with running mate Sine Kerr, a former state senator. He previously served in the Arizona House and Senate, including as Senate President, and chaired the House Freedom Caucus for two years.

background.text: Arizona native with a B.A. in Asian Studies from Brigham Young University, an M.A. in political science from Arizona State University and a J.D. from the University of Arizona; retired attorney.
Served eight years in the Arizona House and six years in the Arizona Senate, and was elected Senate President in 2012.
Elected to the U.S. House in 2016; chairs the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Federal Government Surveillance, sits on House Oversight, and co-chairs the Border Security Caucus.

priorities.text: Affordability: eliminating the state income tax and working with local entities to reduce property taxes.
Housing: streamlining state-level bureaucracy and working with local governments to lower permitting barriers for new homes.
Public safety: encouraging state and local participation in the federal 287(g) immigration program and funding school security.
Water and energy: a long-term water strategy built around Colorado River allocations, and pursuing nuclear and other reliable energy sources.
Education: protecting Empowerment Scholarship Accounts and opting into the federal education tax credit.

positions.summary: Proposes eliminating the state income tax and working to reduce property taxes.
Pledges to protect Empowerment Scholarship Accounts so families can choose the educational method that best meets their child's needs.

Calls for state and local participation in the federal 287(g) program; as a House member voted yes on the Laken Riley Act, which requires federal detention of certain immigrants charged with theft and related crimes.
Would repeal Gov. Hobbs's executive order prioritizing wind and solar on state land while pursuing reliable, affordable energy sources including nuclear.

record.text: Voted yes on the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which passed the House 263–156.
Voted yes on the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which passed the House 220–208.
Voted yes on H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act) when the House voted to concur in the Senate amendment, 218–214.
Voted no on the Inflation Reduction Act (H.R. 5376), which passed the House 220–207.

candidates.name: Risa Lombardo
candidates.ballotNote: Green Party nominee, running with Lisa Castillo; won the Green primary with 67% of votes cast.

summary.text: Risa Lombardo is the Arizona Green Party nominee for governor and a former Arizona Republican Party precinct committee member. She won the Green primary over write-in candidates. She says she would stop data centers, end the use of Flock cameras and work against climate change.

background.text: Former precinct committee member for the Arizona Republican Party.

The Arizona Green Party has disavowed her candidacy, accusing her of being a Republican running to draw votes from Gov. Hobbs. Lombardo told the Arizona Mirror in April that she had been a Democrat most of her life and had been registered with both parties.

Allegation, not a charge: the Arizona Mirror reported on Sept. 1, 2026 that the Attorney General's office opened a criminal investigation into reported campaign-finance fraud involving her Clean Elections qualifying contributions, and that the Clean Elections Commission had ordered its director to complete an investigation and recommend whether she must repay public funds. Six voters told the Mirror they had not made contributions listed in their names. At a Clean Elections Commission meeting, her attorney, Tim La Sota, characterized the investigations and accusations as conspiracy theories.

priorities.text: Says she will stop data centers, end the use of Flock cameras and battle climate change.
Equal opportunity based on individual merit; fair and transparent elections; a responsible environmental plan to protect air and water; and reforms in education, homelessness and the prison system.

candidates.researchNotes: Her campaign site (risalombardo.com) has a short About page and an Issues page that reproduces the Green Party of the United States' four pillars and ten key values; that text is national party-platform wording rather than her own, so it is not quoted. No questionnaire answers with text were found (an AZPM survey lists a Yes on a data-center moratorium without explanation). No site text of her own on abortion, guns, immigration, taxes, housing, schools or the other listed issues. The Arizona Green Party has disavowed her candidacy (see background).

candidates.name: Teri Hourihan

summary.text: Teri Ann Hourihan, a therapist, is the No Labels Party nominee for governor with running mate Angela Harrolle Mohan, a real estate broker. She won the No Labels primary 56% to 44% over Hugh Lytle.

background.text: Therapist; named Angela Harrolle Mohan, a real estate broker, as her running mate on August 6, 2026.

priorities.text: Says she entered the race over problems surrounding health care and will not accept PAC or AIPAC donations.
Affordability and cost of living, including attainable housing and no tax increases.
priorities.quote: keeping my commitment to no tax increases

priorities.text: Water security: conservation, recycling and reuse, new water sources and rural groundwater protections.
Agency reform: audits of state agencies for fraud, waste, abuse and duplication, with more transparency and accountability.

positions.summary: Says she supports protecting school choice, including the Empowerment Scholarship Account (ESA) program, while auditing public, charter, private and ESA-funded programs.
positions.quote: As a candidate for Governor of Arizona, I support protecting school choice while also addressing the broader challenges facing our education system.

statements.quote: I respect the will of the voters and will not seek to overturn the abortion laws that Arizonans have approved at the ballot box.
statements.context: On her campaign site; she adds that she may support changes to current policy through the democratic process

statements.quote: We need effective law enforcement at both the state and federal levels, and our country must have a lawful, functional system for managing immigration.
statements.context: On her campaign site, in a post saying she does not support abolishing ICE and that officers who commit crimes should be held accountable

statements.quote: I would increase housing supply by reducing unnecessary permitting delays and regulatory barriers, supporting infrastructure for new housing, and expanding attainable starter homes, rentals, and workforce housing.
statements.context: In her AZPM candidate survey response

statements.quote: I support expanding access through a long-term plan that combines existing state and federal resources, employer incentives, public-private partnerships, and support for childcare providers.
statements.context: In her AZPM candidate survey response; she adds that this should happen without “simply creating another expensive government program or raising taxes”

statements.quote: Arizona should consider using state funding to prevent dangerous gaps in care—but it should not simply replace every lost federal dollar.
statements.context: In her AZPM candidate survey response on offsetting federal Medicaid cuts; she says she would first audit AHCCCS spending

statements.quote: When the sport is not a co-ed sport, the sport will be only for at birth sexual orientation.
statements.context: On the Equality for All page of her campaign site (wording as published)

candidates.researchNotes: Campaign site (teriann4azgov.org) has issue pages on education, abortion, immigration, taxes, healthcare and others, mixing her own statements with news-linked posts; some pages repeat draft-style text, and only sentences in her first-person voice were quoted. Her AZPM survey responses supplied the housing, childcare and Medicaid statements. No site or survey text found on guns, minimum wage, climate, tariffs or the other listed issues.

researchNotes: Running mates are listed in each candidate's ballotNote rather than as separate entries. The four-candidate slate and all four running mates (Hobbs/Giles, Biggs/Kerr, Lombardo/Castillo, Hourihan/Harrolle Mohan) match the printed Maricopa County sample ballot for Nov. 3, 2026 (a copy hosted by the City of Scottsdale); Ballotpedia and the Arizona Secretary of State site were blocked. Wikipedia lists Castillo as having failed to qualify at the primary stage, but it also lists her as Lombardo's running mate on the general-election ticket and the printed ballot shows her. A Libertarian candidate (Barry Hess) failed to qualify. Hobbs's and Biggs's issue positions come from official government pages and campaign materials; only positions stated directly there are listed. Federal key votes for Biggs and campaign-finance figures are expected to be added by script. Primary-result percentages come from Wikipedia's results tables (citing state returns).
